title: Do R&D advisors charge if no credit is found?
description: Do R&D tax advisors charge fees if no credit is found? It depends on the fee model.
summary: Do R&D tax advisors charge fees if no credit is found? It depends on the fee model. For U.S. businesses claiming the IRC Section 41 credit, generalist CPAs billing hourly or unconditional fixed fees must be paid regardless, while specialist advisors using contingency or benefit-based fixed fees typically charge nothing when no defensible credit is identified.

body.text: Do R&D tax advisors charge fees if no credit is found? It depends on the fee model. For U.S. businesses claiming the IRC Section 41 credit, generalist CPAs billing hourly or unconditional fixed fees must be paid regardless, while specialist advisors using contingency or benefit-based fixed fees typically charge nothing when no defensible credit is identified.
Executive Thesis and Scope

Whether a corporate taxpayer incurs professional advisory fees when an exploratory assessment identifies no viable Research and Development (R&D) tax credit under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 41 (26 U.S.C. § 41) depends on the advisor's regulatory classification, scope of practice, and contractual billing architecture. Generalist tax practitioners—such as Certified Public Accountants (CPAs) and Enrolled Agents performing routine tax compliance and original return preparation—typically bill via hourly rates or unconditional fixed fees because professional ethics codes and federal practice regulations restrict contingent fee arrangements on original tax returns (AICPA Code of Professional Conduct ET § 1.510.001; Treasury Department Circular No. 230, 31 C.F.R. § 10.27). Under those traditional compliance engagements, the corporate taxpayer bears the full financial discovery risk and must pay for all accrued professional hours—such as reviewing prior tax returns, Form W-2 box 1 wage records, and general ledger accounts—even if no activities satisfy the statutory IRC Section 41 requirements. Conversely, specialized R&D tax advisory firms structure exploratory engagements around contingency-based or benefit-based fixed-fee arrangements that shift financial discovery risk away from the client, charging zero professional fees if no defensible R&D tax credit is found.
1. Regulatory Frameworks Governing R&D Tax Advisory Fees
1.1 Treasury Department Circular 230 and Judicial Limits on IRS Fee Regulation

In baseline industry commentary, the prohibition against contingent fees for generalist tax practitioners is frequently attributed to Treasury Department Circular No. 230, often characterized broadly as classifying contingent fees tied to specific tax results as "disreputable conduct."

items: Statutory and Regulatory Placement: Within Circular 230, fee restrictions and contingent fee rules are codified specifically in Section 10.27 ("Fees"), whereas "Incompetence and disreputable conduct" is separately codified in Section 10.51. Under 31 C.F.R. § 10.27(a), a practitioner may not charge an unconscionable fee in connection with any matter before the Internal Revenue Service. Under 31 C.F.R. § 10.27(b)(1), except as provided in paragraphs (b)(2), (3), and (4), a practitioner may not charge a contingent fee for services rendered in connection with any matter before the Internal Revenue Service (such as preparing an original tax return). Under 31 C.F.R. § 10.27(c)(1), a "contingent fee" is defined as any fee that is based, in whole or in part, on whether or not a position taken on a tax return or other filing avoids challenge by the Internal Revenue Service or is sustained either by the Internal Revenue Service or in litigation, including any fee arrangement in which the practitioner will reimburse the client for all or a portion of the client's fee in the event that a position is challenged or not sustained. Charging a prohibited contingent fee violates the practice standards of Subpart B (§ 10.27) rather than being defined verbatim as "disreputable conduct" under Subpart C (§ 10.51).

Codified Regulatory Exceptions under Section 10.27(b)(2)–(4): Under the express text of 31 C.F.R. § 10.27(b)(2)–(4), a practitioner is explicitly permitted to charge a contingent fee in three specific administrative or judicial contexts:

Services rendered in connection with the Service's examination of, or challenge to, an original tax return, or an amended return or claim for refund or credit where the amended return or claim for refund or credit was filed within 120 days of the taxpayer receiving a written notice of the examination of, or a written challenge to, the original tax return (§ 10.27(b)(2));

Services rendered in connection with a claim for credit or refund filed solely in connection with the determination of statutory interest or penalties assessed by the Internal Revenue Service (§ 10.27(b)(3)); and
Services rendered in connection with any judicial proceeding arising under the Internal Revenue Code (§ 10.27(b)(4)).

Invalidation of Refund Claim Restrictions in Ridgely v. Lew and Loving v. IRS: Controlling federal judicial precedent directly governs how specialized advisors legally charge contingent fees on R&D refund claims outside of active IRS examinations. Following the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit's landmark ruling in Loving v. IRS, 742 F.3d 1013 (D.C. Cir. 2014)—which held that the Treasury Department's statutory authority under 31 U.S.C. § 330 to regulate the "practice of representatives of persons before the Department of the Treasury" does not extend to mere tax-return preparation—the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia in Ridgely v. Lew, 55 F. Supp. 3d 89, Civil Action No. 1:12-cv-00565 (CRC) (D.D.C. July 16, 2014) invalidated 31 C.F.R. § 10.27 insofar as it prohibited CPAs and other practitioners from charging contingent fees for preparing and filing "Ordinary Refund Claims" prior to adversarial IRS representation. The court permanently enjoined the IRS from enforcing Circular 230's contingent fee prohibition against the preparation and filing of ordinary refund claims. However, under the AICPA Code of Professional Conduct ET § 1.510.001 ("Contingent Fees Rule") and ET § 1.510.010 ("Tax Matters"), CPAs in public practice remain ethically barred by professional licensing and membership standards from preparing an original or amended tax return or claim for a tax refund for a contingent fee unless the practitioner can demonstrate a reasonable expectation at the time of a fee arrangement that a government agency will provide substantive consideration of the subject matter—an expectation that is explicitly not considered reasonable when the member prepares the client's original tax returns.

body.text: 1.2 Risk Allocation Across Generalist and Specialist Fee Models

Analysis: Because generalist CPAs preparing a client's original income tax return are bound by AICPA Rule 1.510.001 (alongside state board of accountancy rules modeled on the AICPA Code) and the unchallenged portions of Circular 230 § 10.27(b)(1), they structure R&D eligibility assessments under standard hourly billing or unconditional fixed-fee contracts. When a generalist firm reviews prior tax returns, Form W-2 box 1 wages, and general ledger accounts and finds no qualifying activities under 26 U.S.C. § 41, the taxpayer must still pay the accrued hourly or unconditional contract fees in full. Specialist R&D advisory firms, by contrast, either operate on pure contingency models (typically charging 15% to 25% of the credit identified, with 30% generally considered high except for very small claims subject to a minimum fee) or utilize benefit-capped fixed-fee arrangements where no fee is billed if no credit is identified.

headers: Client Financial Exposure If No Credit Is Found

cells: Hourly Billing / Unconditional Fixed Fee (Generalist CPA / EA)
Governed by AICPA Code ET § 1.510.001 and Circular 230 § 10.27(b)(1) for original returns.
High: Client pays for all professional hours expended (e.g., $195–$395/hr at specialist hourly tiers) regardless of whether a credit is found.
Standard for general compliance and hourly consulting; decouples fee from claim size but leaves 100% of financial discovery risk on the taxpayer.
Pure Contingency / Percentage Success Fee (Boutique Specialist)
Permitted for Ordinary Refund Claims post-Ridgely v. Lew or IRS examinations under Circular 230 § 10.27(b)(2); restricted for original-return CPAs under AICPA ET § 1.510.
Zero Upfront Discovery Fee: Advisor typically does not charge if no credit is identified.
Transfers discovery risk to the advisor, but percentage-based fees (e.g., 15%–25% or 30%) create a structural incentive to inflate claims.

body.text: 2. Contingency Fee Conflicts
2.1 The Structural Conflict of Percentage-Based Success Fees

While pure contingency models protect a taxpayer from paying for an unsuccessful exploratory assessment, charging a percentage of the final tax credit introduces an inherent structural conflict of interest. When an advisory firm's revenue scales directly as a percentage of the credit claimed (such as a 25% or 30% success fee), the advisor is financially incentivized to maximize the claim amount by including marginal, poorly documented, or high-risk expenditures, thereby increasing the taxpayer's exposure to IRS examination adjustments, disallowances, and accuracy-related penalties under IRC Section 6662 or erroneous refund claim penalties under IRC Section 6676.
2.3 Statutory Disqualification Triggers That Result in Zero Fee Under the Fixed Fee Approach
During a deep technical and financial tracing engagement, an advisor's audit may reveal that a taxpayer's expenditures are legally ineligible for the R&D tax credit.

items: Failure to Satisfy the IRC Section 41(d)(1) Four-Part Test: Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1), an activity qualifies as "qualified research" only if it meets four cumulative tests applied separately to each business component (26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2)(A)):

Section 174 / Section 174A Eligibility: Expenditures must be eligible to be treated as specified research or experimental expenditures (26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(A); IRS Instructions for Form 6765 (Rev. 12/2025));
Technological in Nature: The research must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature (26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(B)(i));

Business Component Application (Permitted Purpose): The application of the information must be intended to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component (any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention to be held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in a trade or business of the taxpayer) relating to a new or improved function, performance, or reliability or quality (26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii), § 41(d)(2)(B), § 41(d)(3)(A)); and
Process of Experimentation: Substantially all of the activities must constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose (26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(C)).

Cosmetic, Style, or Taste Exclusions: Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(3)(B), research is explicitly disqualified if it relates to style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors. Similarly, routine adaptation of an existing business component to a particular customer's requirement or need is excluded under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(B).

Funded Research Exclusion: Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(H) and 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4A(d), qualified research does not include any research to the extent funded by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person (or governmental entity), which requires evaluating whether payment is contingent on the success of the research (economic risk) and whether the taxpayer retains substantial rights in the research results.

body.text: 2.4 Hypothetical Worked Example: Financial Risk Allocation Under Generalist vs. Specialist Fee Models
The following example is strictly hypothetical and illustrates how the fee formulas and statutory rules operate when no credit is found versus when a valid credit is identified.
Hypothetical Scenario A (No Qualifying Credit Identified):

Assume Corporation X engages an advisor to evaluate $500,000 in engineering payroll and $100,000 in third-party contractor invoices for the 2025 tax year. The technical and financial review consumes 40 professional hours. During contract tracing under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(H), the advisor discovers that 100% of Corporation X's engineering work was performed under cost-plus customer contracts in which the customer bore all economic risk and retained exclusive intellectual property rights, rendering $0 of the expenditures eligible as Qualified Research Expenses (QREs).

items: Model 1 — Generalist CPA / Hourly Consulting Engagement (at a hypothetical $300/hour rate):
Advisory Fee = 40 hours × $300/hour = $12,000
Net Tax Credit Realized = $0
Net Financial Impact to Corporation X = -$12,000
Model 2 — Pure Contingency Advisor (at a 25% contingent fee rate):
Advisory Fee = 25% × $0 credit = $0
Net Financial Impact to Corporation X = $0

body.text: Hypothetical Scenario B (Valid Claim Identified — Comparing Fixed Fee vs. 25% Contingency):

Assume instead that Corporation X's activities are unfunded, satisfy the four-part test under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1), and include $400,000 of Form W-2 wages for three engineers who each spent 85% of their time directly performing qualified research (meeting the 80% or greater "substantially all" threshold under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(d)(2) so 100% of their $400,000 wages qualify) plus $100,000 of substantiated US contractor research payments eligible at the 65% statutory rate under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(3)(A):

items: Total QREs:
Wage QREs = $400,000 × 100% = $400,000
Contract Research QREs = $100,000 × 65% = $65,000
Total Current-Year QREs = $400,000 + $65,000 = $465,000
Regular Credit Computation (assuming a base amount of $215,000 under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(1) and no IRC § 280C(c) reduced credit election):
Excess QREs over Base Amount = $465,000 - $215,000 = $250,000
Gross Section 41 Regular Credit (20% under § 41(a)(1)) = $250,000 × 20% = $50,000
Fee Comparison:

Under the Upfront Fixed Fee Approach ($10,000 quoted fee): Because the $50,000 benefit exceeds the $10,000 upfront fixed fee, Corporation X pays exactly $10,000 (retaining $40,000 net benefit), and the review team receives no financial bonus for pushing marginal expenses into the claim.

Under a 25% Pure Contingency Fee: Corporation X pays 25% × $50,000 = $12,500 (or $15,000 at a 30% contingency rate), and the advisor faces a direct monetary incentive to inflate QREs to increase its commission.

body.text: 3. The "Six-Eye Review" Assessment Process and Internal Risk Controls
3.1 Multidisciplinary Segregation of Duties and the Three Professional Lenses

Adapted from the "segregation of duties" ("N-Eyes") principle used in high-security environments, the Six-Eye Review mandates that every R&D tax credit claim be reviewed sequentially across three distinct professional disciplines—mirroring the structure of an IRS examination team that pairs financial auditors with an IRS Engineering Specialist:

items: First Set of Eyes — Qualified Engineer: Evaluates the technical descriptions and engineering lifecycle to verify technological feasibility, confirm that the activities rely on hard-science principles (engineering, computer science, physical or biological sciences), and ensure the AI or preparer draft reflects engineering reality.

Second Set of Eyes — Scientist: Interrogates the scientific methodology to verify that a systematic, investigative, and experimental study occurred—requiring evidence of hypothesis testing, modeling, simulation, or iterative prototypes rather than routine quality control or post-production debugging—and checks that documentation substantiates the 80% process-of-experimentation threshold under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(6).

Third Set of Eyes — CPA or Enrolled Agent: Audits the financial computations, general ledger cost segregation, and statutory compliance for reporting on IRS Form 6765 (Credit for Increasing Research Activities).

body.text: 3.2 ISO 31000 Risk Management Standards

items: Standard Revision Status (ISO 31000:2009 Withdrawn and Superseded by ISO 31000:2018): ISO 31000:2009 (Risk management — Principles and guidelines, published in November 2009) was officially withdrawn and superseded on February 14, 2018 by ISO 31000:2018 (Risk management — Guidelines) (ISO 31000:2018 Standard Record).

Non-Certifiable Guideline Nature of ISO 31000: Unlike management system requirements standards (such as ISO 9001 or ISO 27001), ISO 31000 is published as a guidelines document rather than a third-party certification standard; as ISO technical documentation states, ISO 31000 "is not intended for certification, regulatory or contractual use" (ISO TC 262 / IEC 31010 Overview).

body.text: 3.3 Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) Governance Over TaxTrex AI

To prevent AI "hallucinations" or misclassifications of routine engineering as qualified research, the Six-Eye team treats the TaxTrex output strictly as a draft: the Qualified Engineer, Scientist, and CPA/Enrolled Agent manually validate the technical narratives and financial figures, rebuilding or rejecting claims that lack substantiation.
3.4 The Financial & Quantitative Rules Audited on IRS Form 6765
During the Six-Eye Review for IRS Form 6765, the review team audits three quantitative and evidentiary compliance areas.

items: The "80% Rule" (Two Distinct Regulatory Provisions Under 26 C.F.R. §§ 1.41-2 and 1.41-4, Plus Section G Business Component Reporting):

80% Wage Inclusion Rule ("Substantially All" Employee Services — 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(d)(2)): Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(B) and 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(d)(2), if "substantially all" of the services performed by an employee for the taxpayer during the taxable year consist of qualified services (engaging in qualified research or directly supervising or supporting qualified research), then all (100%) of the employee's wages for that year qualify as in-house research expenses. Treasury Regulation 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(d)(2) defines "substantially all" as at least 80 percent of the wages paid to or incurred for the employee during the taxable year. If an employee falls below the 80% threshold, only the actual proportion of wages attributable to qualified services may be included.

80% Process of Experimentation Rule ("Substantially All" Research Activities — 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(6)): Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(C) and 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(6), the statutory requirement that "substantially all" of the activities of a research project constitute elements of a process of experimentation is satisfied only if 80 percent or more of a taxpayer's research activities (measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis) constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose.

Form 6765 Section G "80%/Top 50" Business Component Reporting Rule (Effective 2024–2026): In addition, on the redesigned IRS Form 6765 (Rev. December 2024 / January 2025) and Instructions (Rev. December 2025), Section G requires taxpayers (unless exempt as a Qualified Small Business under IRC § 41(h)(3) checking the box to claim the payroll tax credit, or qualifying under the small-filer exception with controlled-group QREs of $1.5 million or less and average annual gross receipts of $50 million or less for the prior three tax years on an original return) to report business component details in descending order of QREs until reaching 80% of total QREs or a maximum of 50 business components (optional for all filers for tax years beginning before 2026, and mandatory for tax years beginning after 2025, i.e., beginning in tax year 2026) (IRS Instructions for Form 6765).
Fixed-Base Percentage and Base Amount Calculations (26 U.S.C. § 41(c)):

Under Section A (Regular Credit) of Form 6765 and 26 U.S.C. § 41(a)(1) and § 41(c), the Regular Credit equals 20% of the excess of current-year QREs over the "base amount." The base amount is the product of the taxpayer's fixed-base percentage (capped at a statutory maximum of 16% under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(3)(C), or start-up percentages starting at 3% for the first five qualifying years under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(3)(B)) and the taxpayer's average annual gross receipts for the four preceding taxable years, subject to the minimum base amount floor of 50% of current-year QREs (26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(2)). Alternatively, taxpayers may elect the Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) in Section B of Form 6765 under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(4), which equals 14% of QREs exceeding 50% of the average QREs for the three preceding taxable years (or 6% of current-year QREs if the taxpayer had no QREs in any of the three preceding taxable years).
Contractor Expenses, the 65% Rule, and Contemporaneous Documentation Nexus (26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(3) and 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(e)):

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(3)(A), a taxpayer may include 65% of amounts paid or incurred to any non-employee for qualified research performed on behalf of the taxpayer (increased to 75% for payments to a qualified research consortium under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(3)(C) and 100% for eligible energy research conducted by universities, federal laboratories, or eligible small businesses under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(3)(D)).

Under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(e)(2), an expense qualifies as contract research only if the agreement is entered into prior to the performance of the qualified research, specifies that research be performed on behalf of the taxpayer, and places the economic risk on the taxpayer while granting substantial rights to the research results. Furthermore, under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(3)(B), prepaid contract research amounts are treated as paid or incurred only in the taxable year in which the research is actually conducted. During the Six-Eye Review, the CPA or Enrolled Agent scrubs vendor invoices, Statements of Work (SOWs), Form 1099-NEC records, and technical logs to verify this nexus before applying the 65% statutory cap, disqualifying any contractor costs that lack prior written agreements or fail the economic risk test.

body.text: If rejecting those ineligible projects leaves no claimable R&D tax credit under the Fixed Fee Approach, the engagement terminates with no fee billed to the corporate client.
